blocks.html: The thalassaemia syndromes are a group of inherited disorders in which the production of haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells, is disrupted. They are caused by deletions or mutations in the DNA that codes for the haemoglobin chains, and are traditionally divided into two types according to which chain is affected: α-thalassaemia (α-globin chains) and β-thalassaemia (β-globin chains). The α-globin chains are made from the HBA1 and HBA2 genes on chromosome 16, while the β-globin chains are made from the HBB gene on chromosome 11.

Reduced globin production means that less functional haemoglobin is formed, and the resulting imbalance leaves an excess of the unaffected chain. Both the underproduction of haemoglobin and these excess chains lead to anaemia. In α-thalassaemia the anaemia arises mainly from the premature destruction of red cells (haemolysis), whereas in β-thalassaemia it results predominantly from red cells that fail to form properly. The clinical severity of the condition, which ranges from mild to fatal, reflects the degree of imbalance between the α- and β-globin chains.

Historically, thalassaemia was most common in a belt stretching from the Mediterranean and Africa to Southeast Asia. Carrier frequencies rose in these regions because the trait, like sickle cell trait, offers some protection against malaria: it slows parasite growth and speeds the clearance of infected red cells, reducing childhood deaths from the disease. Large-scale population movement in recent decades has spread the condition more widely, and increasing numbers of affected individuals are now found in North America and Europe.

Diagnosis of thalassaemia relies on a combination of a complete blood count (CBC) and haemoglobin analysis. On the blood count, the red cells of an affected person are typically small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic): the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is usually below 80 fL and the mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH) below 27 pg. The red cell distribution width (RDW), a measure of the variation in red cell size, is normal or only mildly raised — a feature that helps distinguish thalassaemia from iron-deficiency anaemia, in which the RDW is usually high. The red cell count itself is often raised.

Because these indices cannot by themselves separate the different causes of small red cells, haemoglobin typing by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) or capillary zone electrophoresis is used to measure the proportions of the different haemoglobins. A raised level of haemoglobin A2 (above 3.5% of total haemoglobin) is characteristic of β-thalassaemia trait. Genetic testing is usually needed to confirm a diagnosis of α-thalassaemia.

Several screening programmes can be offered, including neonatal, carrier, premarital and antenatal screening. Screening is central to prevention, yet provision remains inadequate worldwide, particularly in the regions where the condition is most common.

texts.title: Transfusion, Disease-Modifying Therapy and Iron Overload

blocks.html: Transfusion is a key treatment for the chronic anaemia of severe thalassaemia. Patients are broadly categorised as having transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (TDT) or non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (NTDT). The decision to start a patient on a long-term, regular transfusion programme depends on several factors, including how severe the anaemia is at first presentation, poor growth, and clinical signs of ineffective erythropoiesis such as skeletal deformities.

Beyond transfusion, disease-modifying drugs that target the ineffective red cell production and premature red cell destruction of thalassaemia are available. Two such options are luspatercept, which improves the maturation of red cell precursors, and mitapivat, which acts on red cell metabolism. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation and gene therapy are both approved as potentially curative treatments.

A major concern in long-term management is iron overload. This may arise from repeated transfusions in TDT, or from increased absorption of iron from the gut in NTDT. Over time, iron accumulates in tissues such as the heart and the liver. Unless the excess iron is removed — a process known as chelation — the affected organs are exposed to oxidative stress and are at risk of damage.

items.docHtml: To: All ward staff. Following a recent inspection, concerns were raised about inconsistent temperature monitoring of medication refrigerators across clinical areas. All refrigerators storing vaccines, insulin, and other temperature-sensitive medications must be maintained between 2°C and 8°C. Staff are reminded that temperatures must be recorded twice daily, at the beginning and end of each shift, using the standardised log sheets. If the temperature falls outside the acceptable range, the affected medications must be quarantined immediately and pharmacy contacted for advice – do not assume the medications are safe to use even if the temperature has subsequently returned to normal. Patients should not be discharged before 10:00am unless clinically indicated and the patient has expressed a preference for early discharge, nor after 8:00pm except in exceptional circumstances documented by the responsible consultant. Hand hygiene with soap and water is essential, as alcohol-based hand rubs do not reliably eliminate C. difficile spores. If oxygen saturations cannot be maintained within the target range using low-flow oxygen, the patient may require non-invasive ventilation or escalation to critical care.

paras: Neurological and mental-health conditions affect far more than the people diagnosed with them. They place pressure on healthcare systems, interrupt education and employment, and reduce participation in family and community life. These consequences have acquired new significance as economies become more dependent on cognitive work. The capacity to learn, adapt, solve problems and cooperate is increasingly treated as a productive asset, yet economic models rarely account for how illness, environmental exposure or unequal access to education and healthcare can weaken it. A new international commission argues that brain health should therefore be considered part of a society’s infrastructure.

The proposal uses the term “brain capital” to combine two domains: protection from neurological and psychiatric illness, and the cognitive and emotional skills that allow people and organisations to function. Its authors describe brains as infrastructure because they are foundational, can deteriorate without maintenance and become more valuable when strengthened. The comparison is deliberately provocative. Roads and power networks can be counted and inspected relatively easily; cognitive resilience, creativity or interpersonal trust cannot. Turning the metaphor into policy requires agreement about what should be measured and convincing evidence that these measures relate to social and economic resilience.

Existing analytical tools do not yet provide that evidence reliably. Health statistics may record disease burden without showing how it influences productivity, while economic indicators can undervalue unpaid care, social participation and cognitive wellbeing. The commission also warns that studies often confuse association with causation. A region with better education and stronger economic performance may also report better cognitive outcomes, but this does not reveal which factor produced the others. Unless causal pathways are clarified, an apparently precise model could encourage governments to invest in indicators that are easy to measure rather than interventions that genuinely improve brain health.

The first task is therefore conceptual rather than numerical. Researchers from medicine, neuroscience, psychology, economics, education, environmental science and public policy will attempt to identify which capacities matter and how they interact across the life course. The commission promises participation from the global south so that resilience and productivity are not defined only through models developed in wealthier countries. This matters because the meaning and value of cognitive skills may depend on social conditions, labour markets and cultural expectations. A universal framework will need enough consistency for comparison without treating different populations as interchangeable.

A proposed Brain Capital Index would then combine health indicators, assessments of cognitive skills, environmental risks and the systems that either support or restrict human development. In principle, a single index could help governments compare needs, allocate resources and evaluate progress. In practice, its reliability will be limited by uneven data. Countries differ in how they diagnose mental and neurological conditions, measure educational outcomes and record environmental exposure. Missing information can make an index appear comparable while concealing large differences in data quality. Transparent methods and explicit uncertainty will therefore be as important as the final score.

Measurement is intended to lead to action. The commission plans policy tools for governments, multilateral organisations and investors, together with pilot programmes demonstrating how the framework might be used. Yet producing reports and dashboards is easier than proving that they change decisions or improve outcomes. Implementation will require priorities, accountable milestones and evaluation of unintended effects. A metric designed to attract investment could, for example, favour interventions with easily demonstrated economic returns while overlooking groups whose needs are substantial but difficult to quantify. Evidence of policy uptake should not be mistaken automatically for evidence of health benefit.

The commission’s governance arrangements attempt to address some of these concerns. Scientific work will be separated from funding control, relationships must be disclosed and methods will undergo external and peer review. Advisory groups representing lived experience, civil society, research and business will provide context without formal authority over scientific conclusions. This structure recognises a tension at the centre of the project: broad participation is necessary for legitimacy and implementation, but a large coalition can also bring competing interests and pressure for rapid, visible results. Independence will depend on how these safeguards operate, not merely on their presence in an organisational chart.

Treating brain health as infrastructure could correct a genuine policy blind spot. It encourages finance, education, labour and environmental authorities to recognise that neurological and mental health are not concerns for health ministries alone. But the concept will earn credibility only if it produces measures that are causally defensible, internationally fair and useful in practice. Brain capital is currently an organising idea rather than a validated economic asset. The commission’s most important contribution may therefore be not a headline index, but a disciplined account of what can be measured, what remains uncertain and which investments improve both health and resilience.

paras: Observational studies often compare people who receive a treatment with those who do not, but these groups may differ before treatment begins. People who seek vaccination can have better healthcare access, stronger preventive habits or greater social support, all of which may also influence dementia risk. Subtle cognitive decline may further reduce a person’s likelihood of seeking preventive care years before diagnosis. Statistical adjustment can account only for factors that have been measured accurately. This “healthy vaccinee” problem makes an association between shingles vaccination and fewer dementia diagnoses difficult to interpret as cause and effect.

Recent studies attempted to improve the comparison by exploiting age-based eligibility rules for a live-attenuated shingles vaccine. blocks.html: The thalassaemia syndromes are a group of inherited disorders in which the production of haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells, is disrupted. They are caused by deletions or mutations in the DNA that codes for the haemoglobin chains, and are traditionally divided into two types according to which chain is affected: α-thalassaemia (α-globin chains) and β-thalassaemia (β-globin chains). The α-globin chains are made from the HBA1 and HBA2 genes on chromosome 16, while the β-globin chains are made from the HBB gene on chromosome 11.

Reduced globin production means that less functional haemoglobin is formed, and the resulting imbalance leaves an excess of the unaffected chain. Both the underproduction of haemoglobin and these excess chains lead to anaemia. In α-thalassaemia the anaemia arises mainly from the premature destruction of red cells (haemolysis), whereas in β-thalassaemia it results predominantly from red cells that fail to form properly. The clinical severity of the condition, which ranges from mild to fatal, reflects the degree of imbalance between the α- and β-globin chains.

Historically, thalassaemia was most common in a belt stretching from the Mediterranean and Africa to Southeast Asia. Carrier frequencies rose in these regions because the trait, like sickle cell trait, offers some protection against malaria: it slows parasite growth and speeds the clearance of infected red cells, reducing childhood deaths from the disease. Large-scale population movement in recent decades has spread the condition more widely, and increasing numbers of affected individuals are now found in North America and Europe.

Diagnosis of thalassaemia relies on a combination of a complete blood count (CBC) and haemoglobin analysis. On the blood count, the red cells of an affected person are typically small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic): the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is usually below 80 fL and the mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH) below 27 pg. The red cell distribution width (RDW), a measure of the variation in red cell size, is normal or only mildly raised — a feature that helps distinguish thalassaemia from iron-deficiency anaemia, in which the RDW is usually high. The red cell count itself is often raised.

Because these indices cannot by themselves separate the different causes of small red cells, haemoglobin typing by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) or capillary zone electrophoresis is used to measure the proportions of the different haemoglobins. A raised level of haemoglobin A2 (above 3.5% of total haemoglobin) is characteristic of β-thalassaemia trait. Genetic testing is usually needed to confirm a diagnosis of α-thalassaemia.

Several screening programmes can be offered, including neonatal, carrier, premarital and antenatal screening. Screening is central to prevention, yet provision remains inadequate worldwide, particularly in the regions where the condition is most common.

blocks.html: Transfusion is a key treatment for the chronic anaemia of severe thalassaemia. Patients are broadly categorised as having transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (TDT) or non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (NTDT). The decision to start a patient on a long-term, regular transfusion programme depends on several factors, including how severe the anaemia is at first presentation, poor growth, and clinical signs of ineffective erythropoiesis such as skeletal deformities.

Beyond transfusion, disease-modifying drugs that target the ineffective red cell production and premature red cell destruction of thalassaemia are available. Two such options are luspatercept, which improves the maturation of red cell precursors, and mitapivat, which acts on red cell metabolism. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation and gene therapy are both approved as potentially curative treatments.

A major concern in long-term management is iron overload. This may arise from repeated transfusions in TDT, or from increased absorption of iron from the gut in NTDT. Over time, iron accumulates in tissues such as the heart and the liver. Unless the excess iron is removed — a process known as chelation — the affected organs are exposed to oxidative stress and are at risk of damage.

paras: Neurological and mental-health conditions affect far more than the people diagnosed with them. They place pressure on healthcare systems, interrupt education and employment, and reduce participation in family and community life. These consequences have acquired new significance as economies become more dependent on cognitive work. The capacity to learn, adapt, solve problems and cooperate is increasingly treated as a productive asset, yet economic models rarely account for how illness, environmental exposure or unequal access to education and healthcare can weaken it. A new international commission argues that brain health should therefore be considered part of a society’s infrastructure.

The proposal uses the term “brain capital” to combine two domains: protection from neurological and psychiatric illness, and the cognitive and emotional skills that allow people and organisations to function. Its authors describe brains as infrastructure because they are foundational, can deteriorate without maintenance and become more valuable when strengthened. The comparison is deliberately provocative. Roads and power networks can be counted and inspected relatively easily; cognitive resilience, creativity or interpersonal trust cannot. Turning the metaphor into policy requires agreement about what should be measured and convincing evidence that these measures relate to social and economic resilience.

Existing analytical tools do not yet provide that evidence reliably. Health statistics may record disease burden without showing how it influences productivity, while economic indicators can undervalue unpaid care, social participation and cognitive wellbeing. The commission also warns that studies often confuse association with causation. A region with better education and stronger economic performance may also report better cognitive outcomes, but this does not reveal which factor produced the others. Unless causal pathways are clarified, an apparently precise model could encourage governments to invest in indicators that are easy to measure rather than interventions that genuinely improve brain health.

The first task is therefore conceptual rather than numerical. Researchers from medicine, neuroscience, psychology, economics, education, environmental science and public policy will attempt to identify which capacities matter and how they interact across the life course. The commission promises participation from the global south so that resilience and productivity are not defined only through models developed in wealthier countries. This matters because the meaning and value of cognitive skills may depend on social conditions, labour markets and cultural expectations. A universal framework will need enough consistency for comparison without treating different populations as interchangeable.

A proposed Brain Capital Index would then combine health indicators, assessments of cognitive skills, environmental risks and the systems that either support or restrict human development. In principle, a single index could help governments compare needs, allocate resources and evaluate progress. In practice, its reliability will be limited by uneven data. Countries differ in how they diagnose mental and neurological conditions, measure educational outcomes and record environmental exposure. Missing information can make an index appear comparable while concealing large differences in data quality. Transparent methods and explicit uncertainty will therefore be as important as the final score.

Measurement is intended to lead to action. The commission plans policy tools for governments, multilateral organisations and investors, together with pilot programmes demonstrating how the framework might be used. Yet producing reports and dashboards is easier than proving that they change decisions or improve outcomes. Implementation will require priorities, accountable milestones and evaluation of unintended effects. A metric designed to attract investment could, for example, favour interventions with easily demonstrated economic returns while overlooking groups whose needs are substantial but difficult to quantify. Evidence of policy uptake should not be mistaken automatically for evidence of health benefit.

The commission’s governance arrangements attempt to address some of these concerns. Scientific work will be separated from funding control, relationships must be disclosed and methods will undergo external and peer review. Advisory groups representing lived experience, civil society, research and business will provide context without formal authority over scientific conclusions. This structure recognises a tension at the centre of the project: broad participation is necessary for legitimacy and implementation, but a large coalition can also bring competing interests and pressure for rapid, visible results. Independence will depend on how these safeguards operate, not merely on their presence in an organisational chart.

Treating brain health as infrastructure could correct a genuine policy blind spot. It encourages finance, education, labour and environmental authorities to recognise that neurological and mental health are not concerns for health ministries alone. But the concept will earn credibility only if it produces measures that are causally defensible, internationally fair and useful in practice. Brain capital is currently an organising idea rather than a validated economic asset. The commission’s most important contribution may therefore be not a headline index, but a disciplined account of what can be measured, what remains uncertain and which investments improve both health and resilience.

🎓

How to use this drill

An interactive scanning workout for OET Reading Part A.

  1. 1Pick a text (A–D) and press “Start Drill”. This shuffles that text’s cues into a fresh, random order.
  2. 2Read the cue. It shows the meaning of a word — never the word itself.
  3. 3Press “Start Timer” for the 20-second challenge. Optional, but great for building speed under pressure.
  4. 4Click the word in the text that matches the cue. Every word is clickable, so you must truly scan to find it.
  5. 5Watch the colour feedback. Green = correct. Red = try again. Amber = the answer was revealed for you.
  6. 6Reveal or move on. The answer auto-highlights when the timer ends, or press “Reveal Answer”. Use “Next Cue” to continue and “Reset Text” to start over.
Correct Try again Revealed
Student tipDon’t read top to bottom. Jump around — beginnings, middles, table cells, flowchart steps and notes.

For students

For teachers

A

Safe Medication Administration

Clinical paragraph

Safe medication administration protects patients from avoidable harm. Before giving any drug, the nurse must verify the patient's identity against the wristband and the prescription chart. Confirm the correct drug, dose, route and time, and check that the medication has not expired. If the handwriting on the chart is illegible or the order seems unusual, clarify it with the prescriber rather than guessing. High-risk drugs such as insulin, anticoagulants and opioids require an independent second check by a colleague.

Allergies must always be reviewed before administration; a documented allergy should be treated as an absolute contraindication. Explain the purpose of the medicine to the patient and obtain their consent. Watch for early signs of an adverse reaction, such as a rash, itching or breathlessness, and stop at once if one appears. Any drug that is withheld or refused must be recorded, together with the reason.

Controlled drugs demand particular care. Two staff must witness the count, and any discrepancy in the register has to be investigated immediately. When a dose is due but the patient is absent or nil by mouth, do not simply omit it without informing the team. Finally, sign the chart only after the medicine has actually been swallowed or given, never in advance, so that the record stays accurate.

B

Early Warning Score Response

Paragraph + table

National Early Warning Score (NEWS) — Response Thresholds

The National Early Warning Score, or NEWS, helps staff to detect deterioration early by giving a number to each vital sign. The individual scores are added together to give a total, which then guides how often the patient is observed and who should be informed. A single very high reading in one parameter matters as much as a high overall score, so never disregard an extreme value.

Aggregate scoreRiskMonitoring frequencyRequired response
0Low12-hourlyContinue routine care
1 – 4Low4 – 6 hourlyInform the nurse, who will assess the patient
3 in one parameterLow – medium1-hourlyNurse to review and consider escalation
5 – 6Medium1-hourlyUrgent review by the ward doctor
7 or moreHighContinuousEmergency assessment by the critical care team

Whenever the score rises, increase the frequency of observations without waiting for the next routine round. Document the actions taken and the patient's response promptly. If the expected senior review does not materialise within the stated time, the nurse must escalate further up the chain. Above all, trust clinical judgement: if a patient looks unwell, act even when the numbers appear reassuring.

C

Acute Stroke Pathway

Paragraph + flowchart

Recognition and Management of Acute Stroke

A stroke occurs when the blood supply to part of the brain is suddenly interrupted, and every minute of delay costs surviving brain tissue. Rapid recognition using the FAST test — face, arm, speech, time — allows treatment to begin quickly. The overall aim is to minimise the time between the onset of symptoms and definitive care.

Step 1 — Recognise. Look for a drooping face, arm weakness or slurred speech, and note the exact time the symptoms began.
↓
Step 2 — Alert. Trigger the stroke pathway and pre-notify the imaging department so a scan can be performed immediately.
↓
Step 3 — Assess. Confirm the diagnosis, check the blood glucose and exclude conditions that mimic a stroke.
↓
Step 4 — Image. Arrange an urgent brain scan to establish whether the stroke is caused by a clot or a bleed.
↓
Step 5 — Treat. If a clot is confirmed and the patient is eligible, give clot-busting treatment, known as thrombolysis, within the agreed window.
↓
Step 6 — Admit. Transfer the patient to a specialist stroke unit for close surveillance.

Throughout, keep the patient nil by mouth until a swallow assessment has been carried out, because an unsafe swallow can lead to aspiration. Monitor the blood pressure carefully, as very high levels may need to be lowered cautiously. Involve the family early and explain each step, since the situation can be distressing. Early rehabilitation, begun as soon as the patient is stable, greatly improves the chance of a good recovery.

D

Falls Prevention & Safe Discharge

Mixed: headings · bullets · data

Preventing Falls in Hospital

Falls are among the most common patient-safety incidents and can cause serious injury, especially in older people. A structured approach reduces the risk considerably.

On admission

  • Screen every patient for their risk of falling, and repeat the check after any change in condition.
  • Ask about previous falls, dizziness and problems with mobility.
  • Review the medication list for drugs that cause drowsiness or lower the blood pressure.

Keeping patients safe

  • Keep the call bell, water and glasses within easy reach.
  • Ensure the floor is free of clutter and that any spillage is wiped up at once.
  • Provide non-slip footwear and adequate lighting, particularly at night.
  • Answer call bells without delay to discourage patients from getting up alone.

Quick reference

Risk screen: within 6 hours  ·  Bed rails: only after assessment  ·  Hourly rounding: for high-risk patients  ·  Footwear: non-slip, correct size

Before discharge

  • Confirm the patient can walk safely and manage stairs, using a walking aid if needed.
  • Arrange any equipment for the home and a referral to physiotherapy.
  • Give written advice and check the patient knows when to seek help.
Note: Report every fall, however minor, and examine the patient for injuries before moving them. A patient who has fallen and cannot be fully assessed should be treated as though a fracture is present until proven otherwise. Never leave a high-risk patient unattended in the bathroom.

readingArticle.title: Rebalancing the Brain in Huntington's Disease
readingArticle.standfirst: The genetic cause of Huntington's has been known for decades. A study in mice suggests that easing its symptoms may turn less on the faulty gene than on the brain circuits it throws out of balance.
readingArticle.bodyText:
Huntington's disease is among the cruellest disorders in medicine: an inherited, incurable condition that steadily strips its sufferers of controlled movement. In one respect it ought to be tractable, for its cause is singular and well established — a single faulty gene, passed from parent to child. Yet knowing the cause has proved a long way from understanding the illness. A recent study in mice takes a different tack, turning attention from the gene itself to the brain circuits it disrupts.

The circuits in question sit in the motor cortex and its connections to the striatum, a deep region that helps orchestrate movement. What the researchers examined were the cortex's inhibitory neurons — the cells whose task is to restrain the excitatory neurons around them. One, known as VIP, has an unusual remit: rather than quieting excitatory cells directly, it inhibits other inhibitory neurons, in effect releasing the brake on the brake.

Recording the activity of these neurons in affected mice as the animals moved, the team uncovered a lopsided signature. The VIP cells, which should have been engaged during movement, fell almost silent; the other inhibitory subtypes grew overactive; and the excitatory neurons that carry the cortex's instructions onward were themselves subdued. A disorder of movement, in other words, might trace in part to a single quiet class of cell.

A result seen in only one strain of mouse invites the suspicion that it is a quirk of that model. To guard against this, the researchers turned to a second strain in which the disease unfolds more slowly, and found the same core signature — milder, but unmistakably present. With the disturbance traced upstream to the VIP neurons, those cells became the natural place to intervene.

readingArticle.title: The Limits of Sunscreen
readingArticle.standfirst: "Wear sunscreen" may be the most repeated advice in skin health. It is also, on closer inspection, among the most misunderstood — and the confidence it inspires can be a hazard of its own.
readingArticle.bodyText:
Few pieces of health advice are repeated as confidently, or as universally, as the instruction to wear sunscreen. It has acquired something of the force of a moral duty: to apply it is to be responsible, to neglect it faintly reckless. Yet the very simplicity that makes the message so easy to broadcast may also be its weakness. Treated as a shield, sunscreen can quietly license the sun exposure it is meant to guard against; and a message built around a single product tends to obscure a more awkward truth — that protecting the skin is a matter of weighing the sun's real harms against its real benefits. The slogan, in short, may mislead almost as readily as it protects.

Consider the most common misunderstanding. Many people treat sunscreen as though it rendered the sun harmless: apply it thoroughly, reapply every couple of hours, and stay out as long as one pleases. But no sunscreen, however good, blocks all ultraviolet radiation. Over a long day in the open, the fraction it lets through accumulates into a dose large enough to damage the skin — and once that damage is done, no amount of fresh cream will undo it. Reapplication, contrary to a widespread assumption, does not return the protection to its starting point. The honest picture is a hierarchy: shade, clothing and a hat come first, and sunscreen is best understood as a last line of defence for the skin one cannot easily cover.

None of this amounts to a case against sunscreen, and a fair account must say so plainly. The longest and most rigorous trial of its kind, conducted over decades in an Australian town, found that people assigned to apply sunscreen daily were about half as likely to develop melanoma as those who used it only as they saw fit; their skin aged less, and years later they had even suffered slightly fewer deaths from any cause. The evidence that sunscreen works is, in other words, strong. The quarrel is not with the product, but with the belief that the product, on its own, is enough.

Even the protection people imagine they are buying is often more notional than real. The sun protection factor printed on the bottle is achieved only if the cream is applied in the quantity used to test it — for an adult, some seven teaspoons to cover the body, an amount so generous that almost no one manages it. The upshot is that the real-world protection most people obtain falls well short of the reassuring number on the label.

There is, moreover, a cost to diligence that the standard message rarely admits. Sunlight is not only a hazard; it is also the body's main source of vitamin D. The same conscientious daily use of sunscreen that guards against cancer has been shown, in a recent trial, to raise the risk of deficiency. For the scrupulous user, a vitamin D supplement may be the quiet price of following the advice.

The deepest problem, however, lies in the message's claim to hold for everyone. But the balance of risk and benefit is not the same for all. In people with dark skin, the risk of melanoma is many times lower, while the risk of vitamin D deficiency is higher; for them, the blanket rule may do more harm than good. Advice calibrated for one group, it turns out, has been handed to all.

The appeal of the blunt instruction is easy to understand. It is memorable, it is simple to promote, and it errs on the side of caution. But caution always has a direction. By casting the sun as a threat and little else, the message trades one set of risks for another. What presents itself as clarity is, on inspection, a choice about which risks to keep in view and which to let slip from sight.

Sunscreen, then, is neither the villain nor the cure-all that its detractors and its promoters variously imply. Used as one layer among several, on the skin that cannot be covered, it demonstrably reduces harm. The harder task is not to be simply for or against sunscreen, but to hold its benefits and its costs in view together, and to fit the advice to the person rather than the person to the advice.
